overview.body:
**Bestla** (*bestla*) ​— Mother ‌of Odin, ‌Giantess · ​the Giant Grandmother ​of the ​Gods — ​is the ​ancestress at the ‌root of ​the Æsir ​family tree: ‌the daughter ​of the giant ‌Bǫlþorn, wife ​of Borr, ‌and mother ​of [[odinn|Óðinn]], Vili, ​and Vé ​— the ​three brothers ​who slew [[ymir|Ymir]] ‌and made ​the world ‌from his ​body.[^1]

She is ‌one of ​the most ‌consequential minor ​figures in the ‌Norse corpus. ​Snorri's genealogy ​gives her ‌a single ‌sentence, and Hávamál ‌one oblique ​stanza, but ​between them ‌they establish two ​of the ​mythology's deepest ‌facts: that ​the gods descend ​from giant-kind ‌through the ​mother's line, ‌and that Óðinn's ​first initiation ​into spell-song ​came from ​his maternal uncle ‌— 'the ‌famed son ​of Bǫlþorn, ‌Bestla's father'.[^2]

PuniCodex ​presents the ​name as ‌**Bestla**, identical ‌to the ‌ASCII form: the ‌normalized Old ​Norse spelling ‌carries no ​diacritic and no ​distinctive letter, ​so by ‌the project's ​mechanical rule the ​name is ​Tier 2 ‌— nothing ​is lost in ​transit, and ​nothing needs ‌restoring. No ​domain form of ‌the name ​is held ‌in the ​collection: the ‌plain-ASCII bestla.com is ‌registered to ​a third ​party and ​watched for release, ​and the ‌temple is ‌served canonically ​at /bestla/.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 6 (the genealogy of Búri, Borr, and Bestla), ed. and trans. Anthony Faulkes (London: Everyman, 1987).
Hávamál 140 (Poetic Edda), trans. Carolyne Larrington, The Poetic Edda, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2014).
Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Bestla.

the-name.body:
The name ​is attested ‌in Old Norse ‌as **Bestla** ​(a weak feminine, ​genitive *Bestlu*). ​Its etymology ​is genuinely uncertain. ​The most-discussed ‌proposal connects it ​with Old ​Norse *bast*, 'bast, ‌the inner ​bark of the ‌lime-tree', the ​fibre twisted into ‌rope — ​whence a ​reconstructed Proto-Germanic *bastjō-*, ​'she of ​the bast'. Cleasby–Vigfusson ​and Zoëga ‌record the name ​without committing ‌to the etymology; ​Simek treats ‌the bark-derivation as ​the standing ‌but unproven ​guess, and other ‌scholars have ​looked instead to ​words for ‌'wife' or 'embrace'. ‌The lexicon's ‌gloss 'Bark, bast' ​records the ​leading proposal, not ‌a settled ​fact.[^1]

Whatever ​its origin, the ‌name is ​orthographically uneventful: the ​normalized Old ‌Norse spelling is ​plain Latin ‌letters, identical to ​the ASCII ​form. By the ​project's mechanical ​rule, Bestla ‌is Tier 2 ‌— the ​restoration preserves no ‌distinctive feature, ​because the ASCII ​form loses ‌none.

The letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

‌- **b** → ‌**B** — ​Same, capitalized
‌- **e** → ​**e** — ​Same
- **s** ​→ **s** ‌— Same
- ​**t** → ​**t** — Same
​- **l** ‌→ **l** — ​Same
- ​**a** → ​**a** — Same

‌No form ​of the domain ‌is held ​by the project: ‌**bestla.com** is ​registered to a ‌third party ‌outside the collection ​and is ​watched for ​release. The temple ​is served ‌at /bestla/ and ‌claims no ​owned domain.

sources.citation: Cleasby, Richard, and Guðbrandur Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. Bestla, bast.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Bestla.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed pronunciation ‌of the ‌name is ​**/ˈbest.lɑ/** — ​Old Norse ​Reconstruction.[^1]

Phoneme ​by phoneme:

​- **Be-** ‌— Voiced ​bilabial stop ​[b] and ‌short open-mid ​front [e]; ‌stress falls ​on the ‌first syllable, ​as in ​all Old ​Norse words
​- **-stla** ​— Voiceless ‌fricative ​[s], crisp ‌stop [t], ​lateral [l], ‌and the ​short open ‌back [ɑ] ​of the ‌weak feminine ​ending

For ​the modern ‌speaker, the ‌closest approximation ‌is: 'BEST-la' ​— two ​short syllables, ‌exactly as ​the spelling ​suggests; the ‌'e' of ​'best', then ​a light ‌open ​'ah'.

Kindred ‌and historical ​forms of ​the name:

​- **Old ​Norse** — ‌Bestla, daughter ‌of Bǫlþorn, ​mother of ‌Óðinn
- ​**Modern Icelandic** ​— Bestla, ‌unchanged and ‌still registered ‌as a ‌given name
​- **Proposed ‌cognate** — ​Old Norse ​bast, 'the ​inner bark ‌of ​the lime-tree', ​if the ​bark-etymology holds[^2]

‌Bestla is ​Tier 2 ​because the ​ASCII form ‌loses nothing: ​there is ‌no length-mark, ​no thorn, ‌no eth ​to restore. ‌The name's ‌difficulty is ​etymological, not ​phonological — ​it is ​easy to ‌say and ‌hard to ​explain.

sources.citation: Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), phonology and grammar.
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Bestla.

domains.body:
**Bestla**'s sphere ​is ancestry ‌itself: she ‌is the ​mother of ​[[odinn|Óðinn]] and ​the point ​where the ​divine genealogy ‌crosses into ​the giants' ​world.[^1]

### ‌Mother of ​Odin

Snorri's ‌whole account ​of her ‌is the ​marriage and ​the birth: ​Borr 'married ​the woman ​named Bestla, ‌daughter of ​the giant ‌Bǫlþorn, and ​they had ‌three sons: ​the first ‌was called ​Óðinn, the ‌second Vili, ​the third ​Vé'. The ‌chief of ‌the Æsir ‌is a ​giant's grandson ​on the ‌spear-side of ​the world-tree ​— on ‌the spindle-side, ​entirely so.

​### Giantess

‌The þulur ​of the ‌Prose Edda ​count her ​among the ​heiti of ​troll-women: the ‌tradition never ‌forgets that ​the gods' ‌mother belongs ​to the ​old kind.[^2]

‌### The ‌Maternal Line

‌Hávamál 140 ‌makes her ​family the ‌source of ​Óðinn's first ​wisdom: nine ​mighty spells ‌from her ​brother, the ​famed son ​of Bǫlþorn, ‌and a ​draught of ​the precious ​mead.[^3]

### ‌The Seam ​of the ‌Genealogy

Every ​figure of ‌the younger ​mythology — ‌[[thor|Þórr]], [[baldr|Baldr]], ‌[[hermod|Hermóðr]], and ​the rest ​— descends ​from her; ​she is ‌the grandmother ‌of the ​gods themselves.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 6, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur (troll-women's heiti), trans. Faulkes (1987).
Hávamál 140 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

symbols.body:
Bestla ​has no ‌cult ‌regalia and ​no ​iconography; the ​corpus ​attributes nothing ​to ‌her person. ​The ​images ‌that gather ​around ‌her are ​the ‌images of ​her ​function — ​binding, ​descent, and ​transmission:[^1]

‌- **The ​lime-bast ‌rope** — ​If ‌the etymology ​from ‌*bast* holds, ​her ‌name is ​the ​bark-fibre that ‌binds: ‌the ‌cord joining ​giant-kind ​to god-kind, ‌an ​apt if ​unprovable ‌emblem
- ​**The ​genealogy** — ‌Her ​sole attested ‌attribute ​is a ​position ​in Snorri's ​family ‌tree: the ‌line ​where the ‌Æsir ​pedigree ​roots in ‌Jötunheimr
‌- **The ‌nine ‌spells** — ​The ‌songs of ​power ​Hávamál credits ​to ‌her brother, ​[[odinn|Óðinn]]'s ​maternal uncle: ​wisdom ‌descending through ​the ​mother's house[^2]
​- ‌**The draught ​of ‌Óðrǫrir** — ​The ‌precious ​mead Óðinn ‌says ‌he received ​in ​the same ​stanza: ​inspiration accepted ‌among ‌his giant ​kin

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Bestla.
Hávamál 140 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

mythology.body:
Bestla's mythology ​is a genealogy ‌and a stanza — ‌and between them, ​the foundation-claim of ​the whole pantheon.[^1]

​### The Marriage of ​Borr (Gylfaginning 6)

​Snorri's account of ‌the first gods ​runs: the cow Auðhumla ​licked the rime-stones ‌until a man ​appeared, Búri, fair ‌and mighty; Búri's ​son was Borr, who ‌'married the woman ​named Bestla, daughter ​of the giant ​Bǫlþorn, and they had ​three sons: the ​first was called ‌Óðinn, the second ​Vili, the third Vé'. ‌It is the ​mythology's whole notice ‌of her person ​— and it makes ‌the gods half ​giants by the ‌mother's side. The ​three brothers then kill ​[[ymir|Ymir]], carry his ‌body into the ‌middle of Ginnungagap, ‌and build earth, ​sea, and sky from ​it; later, walking ‌by the sea, ​they find two ​trees and give them ‌breath, wit, and ​senses — Ask ​and Embla, the ‌first humans. Everything the ​gods make, Bestla's ‌sons make.[^1]

### ​The Uncle's Nine ​Songs (Hávamál 140)

Her ​second attestation is ​Óðinn's own: 'Nine ‌mighty spells I ‌got from the famed ​son of Bǫlþorn, ‌Bestla's father, and ​I got a ​draught of the ‌precious mead, poured from ‌Óðrǫrir.' The famed ‌son of Bǫlþorn ‌is Bestla's brother ​— Óðinn's uncle on ‌the mother's side. ​Before the hanging ​on the tree ​and the screaming runes ‌of the following ​stanzas, the Allfather's ​first initiation came ​from his giant mother's ‌house.[^2]

### Among ​the Giantess Names ​(the þulur)

The ​rhymed name-lists of the ‌Prose Edda file ​Bestla among the ‌heiti of troll-women, ​alongside dozens of ‌giantesses no surviving myth ​uses. The catalogue ‌keeps her with ‌her own kind ​even as the genealogy ​marries her out ​of it — ​a tension the ‌sources state and never ‌resolve, because they ​saw none.[^3]

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 6–8, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Hávamál 140 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur, trans. Faulkes (1987).

syncretism.body:
Bestla has ​no foreign ‌double and ‌was never equated ​with any ​Roman or Greek ​figure; her ​comparative frame ​is internal to ‌Germanic culture. ​Tacitus records that ​among the ‌Germans a ​sister's sons are ‌held as ​dear as ‌a man's own, ​and that ​some peoples regard ​the bond ​with the ​mother's brother — ‌the avunculate ​— as the ‌most sacred ​tie of ‌all (Germania 20). ​Hávamál 140 ‌reads like the ​mythic charter ‌of that ​institution: the god's ​first teacher ‌is his ‌*avunculus*, the son ‌of Bǫlþorn.[^1]

​Structurally, she belongs ​to a ‌wider pattern ​the mythologies of ​neighbouring peoples ‌share: a young ​divine house ​that must ‌marry into an ​older, chthonic ‌race to ​be complete. The ​Olympians descend ​from Titans and ​marry into ‌their kind; ‌the Túatha Dé ​Danann intermarry ‌with the Fomorians ​they fight. ​The comparison ‌is typological, not ‌genetic — ‌no borrowing ‌is claimed — ​but it ‌clarifies what the ​Norse sources ​state so ​calmly: the Æsir ‌are a ​young dynasty grafted ​onto the ​old giant ‌world, and Bestla ​is the ​graft.[^2] Her kin ​in the ‌pantheon are ​the other giant-blooded ‌members of ​the divine ‌house: [[odinn|Óðinn]] her ​son, [[loki|Loki]] ‌the full jötunn ‌inside the ​Æsir's circle, ​and [[skadi|Skaði]] and ​[[angrboda|Angrboða]], giantesses ​bound by marriage ‌and by ‌offspring to ​the gods.

sources.citation: Tacitus, Germania 20, ed. and trans. J. B. Rives (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1999).
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), on the giant ancestry of the gods.

cultural-legacy.body:
Bestla's ​afterlife is ‌the afterlife ‌of ​a foundation-stone: ​rarely seen, ​always load-bearing. ​The ​nineteenth-century mythographers ‌who rebuilt ​the ​Norse pantheon ‌for the ​modern reader ‌kept ​her in ‌the family ​trees, ​and every ​scholarly handbook ​since ​— Simek, ‌Orchard, Lindow ​— repeats ‌Snorri's ​sentence, because ‌it is ​all ‌there is ​and it ‌cannot ​be omitted.[^1]

​In modern ‌Iceland the ‌name ‌never died: ​Bestla remains ​a ‌registered given ​name, rare ​but unbroken. ‌In ​contemporary Heathen ​and Ásatrú ‌practice ​she is ‌honoured in ​genealogical ​rites as ​the mother ​of the ‌Allfather, ‌and she ​surfaces occasionally ‌in ​fiction and ​games as ‌the giantess ‌ancestress ‌of the ‌gods. Her ​deepest ‌legacy is ​doctrinal rather ​than ​popular: she ‌is the ​mythology's own ​standing ​proof that ‌the Æsir ​are ​not a ​race apart ‌— ​that the ‌gods of ​Ásgarðr carry ‌the ​giants' world ‌in their ‌blood, ​and carry ​it through ​a woman ​the ‌texts almost ‌entirely passed ​over.[^2]

sources.citation: Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Bestla; Orchard, Andy, Dictionary of Norse Myth and Legend (London: Cassell, 1997), s.v. Bestla.
Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Bestla.

archaeology.body:
No ​cult site, ‌votive ‌deposit, ​runestone, or ​named ​image of ​Bestla ​is known; ‌her ​attestation ​is entirely ‌literary, ​and there ‌is ​no evidence ‌she ​was ​ever an ​object ​of worship ​rather ‌than ​a figure ‌of ​genealogy.[^1] The ‌witnesses ​are manuscripts: ‌the ​Codex ‌Regius of ​the ​Poetic Edda ‌(GKS ‌2365 4to, ‌c. ​1270), ​the sole ‌carrier ​of Hávamál ​140, ‌and ​the principal ​codices ‌of Snorri's ​Edda ‌— the ​Codex ​Regius ​(GKS 2367 ​4to, ‌early 14th ‌c.), ​the ‌Codex Wormianus, ​and ​the Uppsala ‌Edda ‌— which ‌preserve ‌Gylfaginning's ​genealogy and ‌the ​þulur that ​list ​her among ‌the ​troll-women.[^2]

​Her father ​Bǫlþorn ‌is equally ​invisible ​to ​the material ‌record. ​The silence ‌is ​consistent with ‌her ​function: ‌Bestla exists ‌to ​anchor a ​family ​tree, and ​family ‌trees ‌live in ​books.

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Bestla.
Gordon, E. V., An Introduction to Old Norse, 2nd ed. rev. A. R. Taylor (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1957), on the manuscript transmission.

meditation.body:
Bestla ​is the ‌patron of ‌everything a ​lineage ​does not ​say about ​itself. The ​Eddas ‌give her ​a sentence ​and a ‌half; the ​mythology ‌then spends ​every remaining ‌page on ​her ​descendants. She ​stands at ​the exact ​seam ‌where the ​official story ‌begins — ​the ‌grandmother behind ​the genealogy, ‌the giant ​inside ‌the gods.[^1]

​That is ​a truer ‌picture of ‌ancestry ‌than any ​pedigree admits: ​the line ‌you ​are named ​for is ‌never the ​whole ​line. If ‌the old ​guess about ‌her ​name is ​right, it ​means the ​bast ‌that binds ‌— bark ​peeled and ‌twisted ​into rope. ​Whether or ‌not the ‌etymology holds, ‌the ‌function does: ​she is ‌the tie ​that ​joined two ​worlds, and ‌the world ​that ​resulted never ​stopped being ‌both. The ​question ​she puts ​to every ‌genealogy is ​the ‌one her ​descendants had ‌to live ​with: what ‌are ‌you prepared ​to owe ​the side ​of ​the family ‌the family ‌does not ​mention?

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 6, trans. Faulkes (1987).

poetic-edda.body:
The ​Poetic Edda's ‌single notice ‌of Bestla ​is one ​of its ​most quietly ​loaded ​stanzas. In ‌Hávamál 140, ​[[odinn|Óðinn]] recounts: ​'Nine mighty ‌spells I ​got from ‌the ​famed son ‌of Bǫlþorn, ​Bestla's father, ​and I ​got a ​draught ​of the ‌precious mead, ​poured from ‌Óðrǫrir.' The ​famed son ‌of Bǫlþorn ​is ‌her brother; ​the stanza ‌therefore records ​the god's ​first initiation ‌into spell-song ‌at ‌the hands ​of his ​maternal uncle ‌— the ​giant side ​of his ‌own ​blood teaching ​the god.[^1]

‌The placement ​matters: the ‌stanza stands ​immediately ​before the ​account of ​Óðinn's self-sacrifice ‌on the ‌wind-swept tree, ​where he ‌takes ​up the ​runes screaming. ‌The poem ‌thus gives ‌the Allfather ‌two educations ​— ‌the uncle's ​songs first, ​the tree's ​runes second ‌— and ​roots the ​earlier ​one firmly ‌in his ​mother's giant ​family. The ​seeress of ‌Vǫluspá ​remembers the ‌same ancestry ​from the ‌other side: ​before the ‌sons of ‌Burr ​lifted the ​lands, there ​was only ​the yawning ‌gap and ‌the giant ​world.[^2]

sources.citation: Hávamál 138–141 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).
Vǫluspá 3–4 (Poetic Edda), trans. Larrington (2014).

prose-edda.body:
The ​Prose Edda ‌is Bestla's ‌principal witness. ​Gylfaginning 6 ​sets out ​the divine ​pedigree in ​one sentence: ‌Auðhumla licked ​Búri from ​the rime-stones; ‌Búri's son ​Borr 'married ‌the woman ​named Bestla, ‌daughter of ​the giant ​Bǫlþorn, and ​they had ​three sons: ​the first ‌was called ​Óðinn, the ‌second Vili, ​the third ‌Vé'. Snorri ​then proceeds ‌immediately to ​the ‌consequences — ​the killing ​of [[ymir|Ymir]], ‌the world's ‌construction from ‌his body, ​the gifts ​to Ask ‌and Embla ​— all ​the work ‌of Bestla's ​sons.[^1]

Skáldskaparmál ​adds the ‌catalogue evidence: ​the þulur, ‌the great ​rhymed name-lists, ​count Bestla ​among the ​heiti of ‌troll-women, the ‌giantesses of ​the old ‌kind. Snorri's ​prose never ​comments on ‌the tension ‌— the ‌mother ‌of the ​gods filed ‌among the ​giants — ​because for ​the tradition ‌there was ​none to ​resolve.[^2] The ​learned framing ‌is his ​own: writing ​a handbook ​of poetry, ‌Snorri needed ​the genealogy ‌precisely because ​the kennings ‌of the ​skalds presume ‌it; a ‌poet who ​calls Óðinn ​the son ​of Bestla's ​marriage-line is ‌invoking the ‌mythology's founding ​fact.

sources.citation: Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Gylfaginning 6–8, trans. Faulkes (1987).
Snorri Sturluson, Edda, Skáldskaparmál, þulur, trans. Faulkes (1987).

runic-evidence.body:
The ​runic corpus ‌contains ‌no ​attestation of ​Bestla: ​no ​runestone invokes ​her, ‌no ​amulet carries ​her ‌name, and ​no ‌inscription ​links a ‌dedicant ​to ​her — ​a ​silence ​she shares ‌with ​the whole ‌jötunn ​genealogy ‌of the ​gods. ‌Her ​father Bǫlþorn ‌is ​likewise ​unattested epigraphically.[^1]

‌What ‌the inscriptions ‌do ​preserve ​is the ‌linguistic ​environment ​of the ‌name. ​The ​element of ‌her ​most-discussed etymon, ‌*bast* ​'lime-bast', ​is an ​ordinary ​word ‌of the ‌Germanic ​material ‌world — ​the ​fibre of ‌daily ‌rope-making ‌— and ‌weak ​feminine ‌names in ​-la ​are ​common across ‌the ​North Germanic ​anthroponymy. ​But ‌the theonym ​itself ​lives ​only in ‌the ​manuscript ‌tradition: in ​the ‌Younger Futhark ​the ‌name ‌would have ​been ​carved ​ᛒᛁᛋᛏᛚᛅ (b-i-s-t-l-a), ​and ‌no ‌such carving ​survives.[^2]

sources.citation: Lindow, John, Norse Mythology: A Guide to the Gods, Heroes, Rituals, and Beliefs (Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2001), s.v. Bestla.
Cleasby & Vigfússon, An Icelandic-English Dictionary, 2nd ed. (Clarendon Press, 1957), s.v. bast, Bestla.

sagas.body:
Beyond ​the Eddas, ‌Bestla's ‌medieval afterlife ​is ​thin but ​consistent. Saxo ​Grammaticus, ​retelling the ‌origins ​of the ​northern ‌gods in ​the ‌opening of ​his ‌Gesta Danorum, ​euhemerizes the ​whole ​divine house ​as ​ancient kings ‌and ​sorcerers and ‌gives ​no corresponding ‌role ​to a ‌mother of ​Odin ‌— a ​reminder ​that the ‌Bestla ‌genealogy is ‌specifically ​the Eddic ​tradition's, ‌preserved by ​Snorri and ​the ‌Hávamál manuscript, ​not ​a pan-Scandinavian ‌datum.[^1]

​The skaldic ‌and ​learned tradition ​keeps ​her alive ​as a ‌genealogical ‌reference point: ​Snorri's ‌þulur file ​her ​among the ‌troll-women, ‌and the ‌pedigree ‌of Gylfaginning ​is repeated ‌wherever ​the Edda's ​prologue-material ​is copied. ‌In ​Iceland the ​name ​passed from ‌mythology ​into the ​living name-pool: ​Bestla ‌is a ​registered ‌modern Icelandic ​given ‌name, one ​of ‌the few ‌figures ​of the ​jötunn generation ​to ​be carried ‌continuously ‌into the ​present.[^2]

sources.citation: Saxo Grammaticus, Gesta Danorum, Book 1, trans. Peter Fisher, ed. Hilda Ellis Davidson (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1979).
Simek, Rudolf, Dictionary of Northern Mythology, trans. Angela Hall (Cambridge: D. S. Brewer, 1993), s.v. Bestla.

original-script.body:
The name ​is preserved ‌in medieval Icelandic ‌manuscripts in ​the Latin alphabet ​as **Bestla** ​— Old Norse ​(North Germanic), attested ​13th–14th c. ‌CE in the ​Codex Regius ​of the Poetic ‌Edda (Hávamál ​140) and the ‌codices of ​Snorri's Edda (Gylfaginning ‌6), recording ​material centuries older.[^1] ​Before the ​Latin bookhand, Old ​Norse names ​were carved in ‌the Younger Futhark; ​no runic ‌attestation of this ​name survives, ‌so the manuscript ​form is ‌the primary witness.

​The scholarly ‌rendering proceeds step ​by step:

​- The name ‌is a ‌weak feminine in ‌*-la*, genitive ​*Bestlu*; its etymology ​is uncertain, with ‌the leading ​proposal connecting it ​to *bast*, ‌'lime-bast'.[^2]
- The ​normalized Old ​Norse spelling is ‌plain Latin ​letters throughout: no ‌acute accent, ​no thorn, no ​eth.
- ​In the Younger ​Futhark it ‌would have been ‌carved ᛒᛁᛋᛏᛚᛅ (b-i-s-t-l-a), ​the ᛁ-rune ‌covering e as ​it covers ​i, since the ‌Viking-Age row ‌does not distinguish ‌the front ‌vowels.
- The ​Unicode form ‌**Bestla** is therefore ​letter-for-letter the ​ASCII form: the ​name is ‌Tier 2 by ​the mechanical rule, ​its restoration ​complete in plain ‌Latin. Because ​the name is ​pure ASCII, ​its domain was ‌registered decades ​ago in the ‌ordinary way; ​**bestla.com is held ‌by a ​third party outside ‌the PuniCodex ‌collection and is ​watched for release** ​— no ​form of the ​name is ‌currently owned, and ‌this temple ​claims none.
